author: blu
body: A lossy or slow peer means a sent segment can vanish and an inbound one can arrive out of order or twice. Three mechanisms make the guest stack survive it, all driven by `net-tick` on the caller's poll cadence (there is no wall clock):

author: blu
body: RETRANSMISSION. `net-send` stashes the data frame it just sent as `rexmit-frame` and the sequence the peer must acknowledge as `rexmit-ack`, arming `rexmit-rto`. An inbound ACK that reaches `rexmit-ack` clears the stash; if `rexmit-rto` counts down to zero first, `net-tick` re-queues the same frame and re-arms. One segment is outstanding at a time -- this stack sends a response, then waits for it.

author: blu
body: TIME_WAIT and LAST_ACK are modelled, not reclaimed by an external idle timeout. On reaching either, `close-timer` is armed; `net-tick` counts it down and drops the connection to CLOSED at zero -- a bounded 2*MSL wait absorbing a lost final ACK.

author: blu
body: RECEIVE WINDOW. A data segment outside the advertised window -- a duplicate of already-delivered bytes, or one starting beyond the window -- is dropped and re-ACKed (`net-process-ip` via `net-seg-acceptable`), so a doubled or out-of-range delivery cannot corrupt the byte stream.

author: blu
body: A segment is demultiplexed before it is stepped. It belongs to this session only if it is addressed to this session's local port; anything else is another connection's traffic and is dropped.

author: blu
body: One connection cannot see this. Two cannot avoid it: a guest that answers an inbound request by opening an outbound one has both live at once, and every frame for either is offered to whichever session happens to be looping.

author: blu
body: WHAT THIS FIX IS NOT. It was written while chasing a `tools/cdx-registry` failure and it did NOT fix it -- proven by neutralising this check and reproducing the failure with it gone, and again by an announce-driven registry that opens no outbound connection at all and fails the same way. An earlier draft of this prose asserted the nesting as that failure's cause. It is not established, and the sentence is removed rather than softened, because a confident wrong cause in a comment is what the next reader will believe.

author: blu
body: The defect this DOES fix stands on its own: a session must not step traffic addressed to a port it does not own.

author: blu
body: THE REMOTE PORT IS PART OF THE CHECK, and it has to be. Matching the local port alone is not enough for a server that handles more than one connection in a row: every one of them is accepted on the same local port, so a stale frame from the connection just closed -- a retransmit, a lingering FIN -- is applied to the FRESH session that replaced it. Measured: `tools/cdx-registry` served its first request correctly, went back to accept, took the second connection, and then sat in its receive loop forever with the second request already on the wire.

author: blu
body: A listener whose `remote-port` is still zero has not yet been claimed by a peer, so it must take any SYN -- that is how it learns who it is talking to (`tcp-step-listening` stores `seg.src-port`). Once claimed, anything from a different source port belongs to somebody else.

author: blu
body: STILL OPEN: a segment for another session is DROPPED rather than queued, because there is no per-session inbox. A frame arriving for a connection that is not the one currently looping is lost, and the sender has to retransmit -- which nothing in this stack does yet. Do not assume that away.

author: blu
body: `net-tick` advances the reliability timers by one step. The caller drives it on its poll cadence (the WebServer sweep does). It re-queues the outstanding data frame into the outbox when the retransmit timer expires, and drops a connection to CLOSED when its TIME_WAIT / LAST_ACK timer expires. A tick that does neither leaves the outbox untouched, so it never drops frames a prior operation queued.
